prompt: What outer-shell electron configuration do all the group 15 elements (N, P, As, Sb, Bi) share?

choices.text: ns2 np3
ns2 np5
choices.why: That is the halogen (group 17) configuration. Group 15 elements have five valence electrons: ns2 np3.

choices.text: ns2 np4
choices.why: That is the chalcogen (group 16) configuration. Group 15 has one fewer p electron: ns2 np3.

choices.text: ns1 np4
choices.why: Ground-state group 15 atoms have a filled ns subshell, ns2 np3.

explanation: All group 15 elements have the outer-shell configuration ns2 np3, where n is the principal quantum number, placing the nitrogen family in the p block. For example, arsenic is [Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p3.

prompt: Which group 15 element is the most metallic, and why?

choices.text: Bismuth, because it has the lowest electronegativity and ionization energy in the group, so it loses electrons most readily
Nitrogen, because it has the highest ionization energy
choices.why: A high ionization energy and high electronegativity make nitrogen the most nonmetallic member of the group.

choices.text: Phosphorus, because it forms the most allotropes
choices.why: Phosphorus is a nonmetal. Allotropy doesn't make an element metallic; low ionization energy and electronegativity do.

choices.text: Arsenic, because it is a metalloid
choices.why: Arsenic is a metalloid, intermediate in character. Metallic character keeps increasing down to bismuth.

explanation: Metallic character increases down group 15. Out of the group, bismuth has the lowest electronegativity and ionization energy (703 kJ/mol), so it is the most likely to lose electrons and is the most metallic. Nitrogen, with the highest electronegativity, is the most nonmetallic.

prompt: Why is N2 so unreactive, making it the stable source from which all nitrogen compounds are ultimately derived?

choices.text: Its two atoms are joined by a strong triple bond; breaking it is highly endothermic (ΔH = +945.4 kJ)
N2 has two unpaired electrons that cancel each other's reactivity
choices.why: N2 has no unpaired electrons. Its stability comes from its strong N≡N triple bond.

choices.text: Nitrogen atoms have a filled valence shell, like the noble gases
choices.why: A nitrogen atom has five valence electrons, not a full shell. In N2 each atom completes its octet by forming a triple bond.

choices.text: The N–N single bond in N2 is unusually strong
choices.why: N2 contains a triple bond, not a single bond. That triple bond is what makes it so hard to break.

explanation: N2 is stable because of its electronic structure: the bond between the two nitrogen atoms is a triple covalent bond, which is strong and hard to break. The enthalpy change for breaking the bonds in N2 is highly endothermic, ΔH = +945.4 kJ.

prompt: The standard Gibbs energy of formation of NO(g) is +86.55 kJ/mol, for 1/2 N2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) → NO(g). What is ΔG, in kJ, for N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g)?
explanation: Doubling the formation reaction doubles ΔG: 2 × (+86.55 kJ) = +173.1 kJ. The positive value means NO does not form spontaneously from N2 and O2 at normal temperatures.

prompt: What happens when a nitride such as Mg3N2 is added to water?

choices.text: The N^3− ion acts as a very strong base, taking protons from water to form NH3 and OH^−
The nitride is oxidized to N2 gas and hydrogen is released
choices.why: Nitride hydrolysis is an acid–base reaction, not a redox one: N^3− + 3H2O → NH3 + 3OH^−.

choices.text: It dissolves without reaction, giving Mg^2+ and N^3− ions in solution
choices.why: N^3− is far too strong a base to survive in water; it is protonated to ammonia.

choices.text: It forms nitric acid, making the solution acidic
choices.why: Nitric acid forms from N2O5 and water. A nitride gives ammonia and hydroxide, making the solution basic.

explanation: Nitrides are compounds of nitrogen with less electronegative atoms, such as lithium and the group 2 metals (3Mg + N2 → Mg3N2), with nitrogen in the −3 state. In water the nitride ion acts as a very strong base: N^3− + 3H2O → NH3 + 3OH^−.

prompt: In the Haber–Bosch process, N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. What mass of NH3, in grams, can be made from 56.0 g of N2 with excess H2? (Molar masses: N 14.01, H 1.008 g/mol.)
explanation: Moles of N2 = 56.0 g ÷ 28.02 g/mol = 1.999 mol. Each mole of N2 gives 2 mol NH3, so 3.997 mol NH3. M(NH3) = 14.01 + 3(1.008) = 17.03 g/mol, so mass = 3.997 mol × 17.03 g/mol = 68.1 g.

prompt: Nitrogen uses oxidation numbers from +1 to +5 in its oxides. What is the oxidation state of nitrogen in dinitrogen trioxide, N2O3?
explanation: Three O atoms at −2 give −6, so the two N atoms together must be +6, or +3 each. Across N2O, NO, N2O3, N2O4 and N2O5 the oxidation state of nitrogen runs +1, +2, +3, +4 and +5.

prompt: Why is nitrogen-15, rather than the far more abundant nitrogen-14, useful in NMR spectroscopy?

choices.text: N-15 has a nuclear spin of 1/2, whereas N-14 has a nuclear spin of 1
N-15 is radioactive, so it can be traced
choices.why: Both N-14 and N-15 are stable. N-15's value in NMR comes from its spin of 1/2.

choices.text: N-15 has six valence electrons
choices.why: Isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons. They differ in neutrons, and here in nuclear spin.

choices.text: N-14 makes up less than 1% of natural nitrogen
choices.why: It's the other way round: N-14 makes up more than 99% of nitrogen on Earth.

explanation: Nitrogen has two stable isotopes. N-14 makes up more than 99% of natural nitrogen. N-15 is used in NMR spectroscopy (including brain research) because, unlike N-14 with a nuclear spin of 1, it has a nuclear spin of 1/2.

prompt: How do white and red phosphorus differ?

choices.text: White phosphorus is made of reactive tetrahedral P4 molecules and must be stored under water; red phosphorus is a polymeric network that is stable in air
Red phosphorus is made of P4 molecules and white phosphorus is a polymer
choices.why: It's the reverse: white phosphorus is molecular P4, while red phosphorus has atoms linked in a network.

choices.text: White phosphorus is nontoxic and red phosphorus is highly toxic
choices.why: White phosphorus is the toxic one; it caused 'phosphorus necrosis of the jaw' in match workers. Red phosphorus is nontoxic.

choices.text: They are different elements that happen to share a name
choices.why: They are allotropes: two forms of the same element, phosphorus, with different structures.

explanation: White phosphorus is a soft, waxy solid made of P4 tetrahedra. It is so thermodynamically unstable that it spontaneously ignites in air, so it is stored under water, and it is toxic. Red phosphorus forms when white phosphorus is heated to 573 K out of contact with air; its atoms are linked in a chain-like polymeric network, making it less reactive, nontoxic and stable in air. That is why safety matches use red phosphorus.

prompt: Which phosphorus allotrope is the most stable, and what is its structure?

choices.text: Black phosphorus, with atoms linked in puckered sheets like graphite
White phosphorus, made of P4 tetrahedra
choices.why: White phosphorus is the most reactive common form; it ignites spontaneously in air.

choices.text: Diphosphorus, P2, a triple-bonded gas
choices.why: P2 is stable only between about 1200 and 2000°C and is very reactive, with a bond energy only half that of N2.

choices.text: Violet phosphorus, made of separate P8 rings
choices.why: Violet phosphorus forms pentagonal 'tubes', and it isn't the most stable form. Black phosphorus is.

explanation: Black phosphorus is the most stable form of phosphorus. Its atoms are linked in puckered sheets, like graphite, so it is also flaky like graphite. Red and violet phosphorus are polymeric too, while white phosphorus (P4) is the reactive molecular form.

prompt: In the P4 molecule of white phosphorus, how is each phosphorus atom bonded?

choices.text: Each P shares three electrons in bonds to the other three P atoms, giving six P–P bonds, and keeps a lone pair at the fourth tetrahedral position
Each P forms a triple bond to one neighbor, like N2
choices.why: Phosphorus forms weak π bonds, so P4 uses single bonds: each P bonds to three others in a tetrahedron.

choices.text: Each P forms five bonds, using all its valence electrons
choices.why: Only three of phosphorus's five valence electrons are shared; the other two remain as a lone pair.

choices.text: The four P atoms form a square ring with alternating double bonds
choices.why: P4 is tetrahedral, not a square ring, and has six P–P single bonds.

explanation: The structure of P4 follows from phosphorus's s2 p3 configuration. Each atom shares three electrons with the other P atoms, giving the six P–P bonds of the tetrahedron, and its lone pair occupies the fourth position of a distorted tetrahedron.

prompt: When P4 burns, how do the products in limited and in excess oxygen differ?

choices.text: Limited O2 gives P4O6, with an O inserted into each P–P bond; excess O2 gives P4O10, with an extra O attached directly to each P
Limited O2 gives P4O10 and excess O2 gives P4O6
choices.why: More oxygen gives the more oxygen-rich oxide: P4O10 in excess O2, P4O6 when the supply is limited.

choices.text: Both conditions give PO2 molecules
choices.why: Phosphorus oxides keep the P4 cage: P4O6 in limited O2 and P4O10 in excess O2.

choices.text: Limited O2 gives P2 gas and excess O2 gives P4O10
choices.why: P2 is made by heating white phosphorus to high temperature, not by burning it. Limited O2 gives P4O6.

explanation: Burning phosphorus with insufficient oxygen (P4 + 3O2 → P4O6) inserts an O atom into each of the six P–P bonds. With excess oxygen (P4 + 5O2 → P4O10) an additional O atom is attached directly to each P. Red phosphorus forms the same oxides when burned.

prompt: P4O10 dissolves in water to give phosphoric acid: P4O10 + 6H2O → 4H3PO4. What mass of H3PO4, in grams, forms from 100.0 g of P4O10? (Molar masses: P4O10 283.9 g/mol, H3PO4 97.99 g/mol.)
explanation: Moles of P4O10 = 100.0 g ÷ 283.9 g/mol = 0.3522 mol. Each mole gives 4 mol H3PO4, so 1.409 mol. Mass = 1.409 mol × 97.99 g/mol = 138.1 g.

prompt: How is elemental phosphorus produced from phosphate rock today?

choices.text: Phosphate rock is heated with sand (SiO2) to give P4O10 and CaSiO3, and the P4O10 is then reduced with carbon to P4
Phosphate rock is electrolyzed in water to release P4
choices.why: P4 would ignite or react under such conditions. The industrial route is a high-temperature reduction with sand and carbon.

choices.text: Phosphate rock is heated alone until it decomposes to phosphorus and oxygen
choices.why: Phosphates are very stable. Sand is needed to make P4O10, and carbon to reduce it.

choices.text: Putrefied urine is distilled, as Hennig Brand did
choices.why: That was the first recorded isolation, in 1669. Modern manufacturers use calcium phosphate and coke instead.

explanation: Crushed phosphate rock and sand react at 1700 K: 2Ca3(PO4)2 + 6SiO2 → P4O10 + 6CaSiO3. The P4O10 is then reduced by carbon: P4O10 + 10C → P4 + 10CO. Hennig Brand's 1669 isolation from putrefied urine is of only historical interest.

prompt: Why is phosphate removed from wastewater, and how?

choices.text: Excess phosphate causes eutrophication, so it is precipitated as insoluble salts such as FePO4 and AlPO4 by adding iron or aluminum compounds
Phosphate is toxic to fish, so it is boiled off as P4 gas
choices.why: Phosphate's harm is indirect: it feeds algae, which die and deplete oxygen. It is removed by precipitation, not evaporation.

choices.text: Phosphate makes water acidic, so it is neutralized with ammonia
choices.why: The concern is eutrophication, not acidity. Fe^3+ or Al^3+ salts precipitate the phosphate.

choices.text: Phosphate is removed by adding more phosphoric acid
choices.why: Adding phosphoric acid would add phosphate. Iron and aluminum salts remove it as insoluble FePO4 and AlPO4.

explanation: Phosphorus fertilizer entering lakes and rivers causes rapid algae growth (eutrophication): plants grow quickly and die, depleting the water's oxygen. Phosphate is removed chemically with ferric chloride, ferric sulfate, aluminum sulfate or aluminum chlorohydrate, forming very insoluble FePO4 (Ksp = 1.3 × 10^−22) and AlPO4 (Ksp = 5.8 × 10^−19), which are filtered out.

prompt: FePO4 dissolves as FePO4(s) ⇌ Fe^3+(aq) + PO4^3−(aq), with Ksp = 1.3 × 10^−22. What is the molar solubility of FePO4 in pure water, in mol/L?
explanation: For a 1:1 salt, Ksp = [Fe^3+][PO4^3−] = s × s = s^2, so s = √(1.3 × 10^−22) = 1.14 × 10^−11 mol/L. Such low solubility is why adding iron salts precipitates phosphate out of wastewater.

prompt: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, why was radioactive 32P used to label DNA and 35S to label protein?

choices.text: Phosphorus is found in DNA but not in proteins, while sulfur is found in proteins but not in DNA
32P is stable and 35S is radioactive
choices.why: Both labels are radioactive; that is how they were tracked. 32P has a half-life of 14 days.

choices.text: Phosphorus is found in proteins and sulfur in DNA
choices.why: It's the reverse: DNA's phosphate backbone contains P, while proteins contain S.

choices.text: 32P has a half-life of a few nanoseconds, ideal for fast experiments
choices.why: 32P's half-life is 14 days, long enough to be useful for analysis. Most other phosphorus isotopes are too short-lived.

explanation: Only one phosphorus isotope, 31P, is stable, but 32P (half-life 14 days) and 33P (25 days) live long enough to mark DNA. Because sulfur occurs in proteins but not DNA, and phosphorus in DNA but not proteins, Hershey and Chase used 35S and 32P to label them. The 32P stayed with the bacteria, showing DNA is the genetic material.

prompt: Why does fluoride help teeth resist decay?

choices.text: F^− ions replace OH^− ions in the hydroxyapatite of tooth enamel, forming fluorapatite
Fluoride replaces the calcium ions in tooth enamel
choices.why: Fluoride is an anion; it substitutes for the hydroxide anion, not the Ca^2+ cation.

choices.text: Fluoride converts the phosphate in enamel to phosphoric acid
choices.why: Fluoride doesn't destroy the phosphate. It replaces OH^− in the apatite lattice.

choices.text: Fluoride reacts with the phosphorus to form white phosphorus
choices.why: White phosphorus is toxic and is not formed in teeth. Fluoride simply substitutes for hydroxide in the apatite.

explanation: Phosphorus occurs in nature as phosphate minerals such as fluoroapatite, chloroapatite and hydroxyapatite, whose arrangement of ions is similar to that in bones and teeth. When the OH^− ions of the teeth are replaced by F^−, forming fluorapatite, the teeth resist decay.

prompt: The second ionization of phosphoric acid, H2PO4^− ⇌ H^+ + HPO4^2−, has pKa = 7.21. A buffer contains HPO4^2− and H2PO4^− in a 2.5 : 1 mole ratio. Using pH = pKa + log([HPO4^2−]/[H2PO4^−]), what is the buffer's pH?
explanation: pH = 7.21 + log(2.5) = 7.21 + 0.398 = 7.61. Because phosphoric acid ionizes in three steps (pKa 2.12, 7.21 and 12.67), mixing its conjugate bases gives buffers over several pH ranges.

prompt: Which group 15 oxide is basic, as expected for a metal oxide?

choices.text: Bismuth(III) oxide, Bi2O3
Phosphorus oxide, P4O10
choices.why: Phosphorus oxides are acidic; P4O10 dissolves in water to give phosphoric acid.

choices.text: Antimony(III) oxide, Sb2O3
choices.why: Antimony(III) oxide is amphoteric, able to act as either an acid or a base.

choices.text: Dinitrogen pentoxide, N2O5
choices.why: N2O5 is acidic: N2O5 + H2O → 2HNO3.

explanation: The oxides become more basic down group 15. Phosphorus oxides are acidic, antimony oxide is amphoteric, and bismuth(III) oxide acts as a base, as expected for a metal oxide.

prompt: Which group 15 element shows the greatest tendency to catenate, forming many ring and cage compounds?

choices.text: Phosphorus, because of its favorable P–P bond enthalpy
Nitrogen, because it forms the strongest bonds
choices.why: Nitrogen's strong bonds are its multiple bonds (N≡N). Catenation follows N < P > As > Sb > Bi, peaking at phosphorus.

choices.text: Bismuth, because it is the largest atom
choices.why: Catenation falls off after phosphorus; bismuth is at the low end of the order.

choices.text: Antimony, because it forms anions like Sb7^3−
choices.why: Antimony can keep element–element bonds in anions, but catenation is greatest for phosphorus.

explanation: Catenation in group 15 occurs in the order N < P > As > Sb > Bi. Phosphorus forms a wide range of ring and cage compounds because of its favorable P–P bond enthalpy.

prompt: How does multiple bonding change from nitrogen to the heavier group 15 elements?

choices.text: Nitrogen forms very strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds (as in N2, CN^−, NO^+); P and As form multiply bonded compounds only when large groups are attached, as in P2R2
All group 15 elements form stable diatomic E2 molecules like N2
choices.why: Only nitrogen does so under ordinary conditions. P2, for instance, is stable only at very high temperatures and is very reactive.

choices.text: Multiple bonds get stronger down the group as atoms get larger
choices.why: Larger atoms overlap less effectively in π bonds, so multiple bonding becomes weaker and rarer down the group.

choices.text: Nitrogen cannot form multiple bonds because it is too small
choices.why: Nitrogen's small size is what makes its pπ–pπ multiple bonds so strong.

explanation: Nitrogen forms very strong multiple pπ–pπ bonds to itself and to neighbors in the same row, e.g., CN^−, N2 and NO^+. Compounds of P and As (and Bi) with multiple bonds can be made only if large groups are introduced into the molecules, e.g., P2R2 and As2R2, and similar Sb compounds are not known.

prompt: The +5 halides of group 15 show a clear pattern. Which +5 halide is unknown?

choices.text: NF5
PCl5
choices.why: Phosphorus +5 halides are well defined, and PCl5 is a stable compound.

choices.text: SbCl5
choices.why: Antimony's pentafluoride and pentachloride are both well defined.

choices.text: BiF5
choices.why: BiF5 exists; fluoride is the only +5 halide known for bismuth.

explanation: The +5 oxidation state halides are unknown for nitrogen, well defined for phosphorus, stable for arsenic only as the fluoride, well defined for the fluoride and chloride of antimony, and known only as the fluoride for bismuth. For both +3 and +5, stability follows F > Cl > Br > I, following the bond enthalpies.

prompt: Which of the group 15 pentafluorides is the strongest Lewis acid?

choices.text: SbF5
PF5
choices.why: PF5 is the weakest Lewis acid of the three; the order is SbF5 > AsF5 > PF5.

choices.text: AsF5
choices.why: AsF5 lies in the middle of the order SbF5 > AsF5 > PF5.

choices.text: NF5
choices.why: NF5 doesn't exist: nitrogen forms no +5 halides.

explanation: The Lewis acidity of the +5 fluorides runs SbF5 > AsF5 > PF5. Coordination numbers likewise rise down the group, with higher coordination numbers observed for Sb and Bi.

prompt: How do the +5 oxides and oxoacids of group 15 compare as oxidizing agents?

choices.text: N(V) and Bi(V) are strongly oxidizing, P(V) is very stable, and As(V) and Sb(V) are mildly oxidizing
All are equally strong oxidants because they share the +5 state
choices.why: The stability of the +5 state varies, even alternating, down the group. P(V) compounds are very stable, while N(V) and Bi(V) are strongly oxidizing.

choices.text: Oxidizing power increases steadily from N to Bi
choices.why: The trend isn't steady: N(V) is strongly oxidizing, P(V) is very stable, then oxidizing power rises again toward Bi(V).

choices.text: P(V) is the strongest oxidant in the group
choices.why: P(V) oxides and oxoacids, like phosphates, are very stable and not strongly oxidizing.

explanation: Stabilization of the +3 state relative to +5 is less well defined in group 15 than in group 14; an alternation is seen. Bi(V) and N(V) oxides and oxoacids are strongly oxidizing, P(V) oxides and oxoacids are very stable, and As(V) and Sb(V) ones are mildly oxidizing.

prompt: Elemental antimony can be obtained from stibnite, Sb2S3. Which reaction from the section does this?

choices.text: Sb2S3 + 3Fe → 2Sb + 3FeS, by melting the sulfide with iron at about 600°C
2SbCl3 + 3H2S → Sb2S3 + 6HCl
choices.why: That reaction makes amorphous Sb2S3 from an antimony trichloride solution; it doesn't give the element.

choices.text: Sb2S3 + 3H2O → 2Sb + 3H2SO3
choices.why: Antimony trisulfide is insoluble in water and doesn't react this way. Iron is used to take the sulfur.

choices.text: Sb2S3 → 2Sb + 3S, by dissolving it in water
choices.why: Sb2S3 is insoluble in water. Iron removes the sulfur as FeS, or the ore is roasted and then heated with carbon.

explanation: Antimony trisulfide (stibnite), the most important source of antimony and the origin of the symbol Sb, melts at 550°C. Melting it with iron at about 600°C gives the element: Sb2S3 + 3Fe → 2Sb + 3FeS. Recovery can also parallel arsenic's: the ore is roasted in air and then heated with carbon.
